I created UdaraKita, a web app that monitors and predicts air quality (US AQI) for 12 Indonesian cities. An XGBoost model predicts tomorrow’s AQI from pollutant data (PM2.5, PM10, ozone, NO₂, SO₂, CO), recent AQI history, and seasonal patterns. Results appear with a health category, a prediction range, BMKG and Open-Meteo weather, an interactive map, and three languages (Indonesian, English, Japanese). I built it with FastAPI and React and deployed it on Vercel.

Results: 11 of 12 cities beat the “tomorrow = today” baseline by at least 15%, with an average error reduction of about 29% (best: Makassar, 39%). Jakarta’s error is 8.9 AQI points versus 11.9 for the baseline. The one city that did not pass (Semarang, 11%) does not show a prediction.

One of the fastest ways to trigger a React hydration mismatch in a Next.js App Router application is a single line of date formatting code.

Everything looks completely normal on your local machine. Then you deploy to production, and the browser console throws a hydration error while dates briefly flicker on mobile screens.

Here is why it happens:
Your Next.js Server Component renders the HTML on a Vercel server running in UTC time. When the user opens the page in Jakarta, Sydney, or London, their browser runs client-side hydration using their local timezone and locale settings.

If your component calls new Date().toLocaleDateString() directly during render, the server output and the browser output do not match. React rejects the mismatch and forces an expensive client re-render.

Here are three clean ways we eliminate timezone hydration bugs in production:

1. Lock the Timezone Explicitly on Both Sides:
Never rely on implicit default locales inside Intl.DateTimeFormat or toLocaleDateString. Pass both the locale and an explicit timeZone parameter (for example, 'en-US' and 'UTC' or a stored user timezone preference from the database) so the server and browser produce the exact same string.

2. Defer Local User Timezone Formatting Until Mount:
If you genuinely need the visitor's local browser clock (like "2 hours ago" or local event times), render a deterministic fallback or ISO date on the server, then update to the local string inside a small isolated client wrapper after mount. Never wrap an entire page in a mounted check just to format a timestamp.

3. Pass Serialized ISO Strings Across Server-Client Boundaries:
Pass plain ISO strings from Server Components into Client Components instead of raw Date instances or pre-formatted strings that drop timezone offsets.

Hydration bugs rarely come from complicated business logic. Nine times out of ten, they come from small assumptions about browser globals like window, Date, or invalid nested HTML tags.

A data centre can have power, cooling and customers, yet still be unable to deliver the computing capacity it sold. CNA's report on the US Commerce Department's 16 November measures raises a contractual issue for Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand, alongside Brazil: who bears the risk when advanced chips or their use require new licences? The measures target advanced-chip transactions and significant remote-compute access for China linked and other restricted entities. Scope, thresholds and exceptions matter. This is not a blanket ban on every customer or chip but gives rise to three pressure points for ASEAN's data-centre ecosystem:

1. PROJECT DELIVERY: Delayed GPU shipments can disrupt fit-out, testing, commissioning and completion dates. Suppliers, developers and contractors may face competing claims for extensions of time, delay damages and additional costs.

2. OPERATING PERFORMANCE: A facility may stay online while being unable to provide contracted GPU capacity. Capacity, availability and utilisation commitments can come under pressure, with service credits, revenue shortfalls and financing consequences.

3. CONTRACTUAL RELIEF: A regulatory restriction does not automatically excuse non-performance. Force majeure, hardship and change-in-law provisions need separate analysis under the contract and governing law. Causation, notice, mitigation and lawful alternatives can decide whether relief is available or a breach remains.

International arbitration is well suited to these cross-border contract disputes: a neutral forum, technically informed tribunals, qualified confidentiality and a framework for enforcing awards abroad. Align clauses across supply, construction and capacity contracts, including urgent relief and compatible provisions for related disputes. 

Nevertheless, arbitration cannot replace an export licence. Cross border regulatory advice, technical understanding, and dispute strategy belong together. 

Businesses should consider asking:
1. Who ultimately owns and controls the customer?
2. Who actually uses the compute, and from where?
3. Does the end use match the customer's business?
4. Could brokers, subleases or remote access change the risk?
5. What happens if ownership, users, location or use changes?

Compliance needs to follow the chain, not stop at delivery. Consider ongoing checks, end-user warranties, audit and usage-record rights, change notifications, regulatory cooperation and workable suspension rights. Allocate responsibilities to those with the visibility and control to discharge them. KPIs should also track verified end users, restricted capacity, unresolved compliance exceptions and revenue exposed to licensing changes. Resolve the risk allocation before the chips arrive.

A 40-Year-Old Gen Z  😄 

Two years ago, I found myself back in a classroom. Not just any classroom. It's The Apple Developer Academy | Indonesia. What on earth was a 40-year-old career woman doing with coding and design?? 😅

Well, here's the story.

I was the oldest learner in my cohort. Most of my classmates were around 20-ish. Young enough to be my children. 😂 One day, a fellow learner casually told me, “Wow Kak Citra, you're the same age as my mom!”
Well, thank you for the reminder. (And yes, it's Kakak, not Ibu!) 😂

But here's the funny thing: despite the age gap, I never really felt old. For a while, I got to live the Gen Z life. Learning together, laughing at things I didn't always understand, listening to Bernadya's songs, discovering new perspectives, and making friends with some of the most brilliant young minds I've ever met.
It was exhilarating. Almost like..... being young again. 
I even had the incredible opportunity to meet Apple's CEO, Tim Cook. Definitely not something I expected when I decided to go back to school at 40!

But beyond the excitement and unforgettable experiences, the Academy taught me something that challenged the way I had been thinking for years.
I had to learn how to unlearn.
After years of professional experience, I had become pretty good at recognizing patterns, making decisions, and jumping straight into solutions. And that's exactly what I had to unlearn. Here, I discovered that defining the right problem is often more important than finding the right solution.
We spent so much time questioning assumptions, talking to people, challenging our initial interpretations, and resisting the temptation to solve things too quickly. It was uncomfortable at times. Because experience can give you confidence. But it can also make you believe you already know the answer before you've fully understood the question. This experience humbling me to a different level  😅 

And here comes the most unexpected thing I found at the Academy: A part of myself I had almost forgotten.
I actually love being a student! 

After years of working, I was so used to being the person who was expected to know things, have answers, and make decisions. But at the Academy, I could ask the most basic questions, admit I had absolutely NO IDEA what I was doing  🤣, and learn from people half my age.

I didn't realize how much I had missed that feeling until I experienced it again. 🥹 

Thank you, Apple Developer Academy | Indonesia, for the friendships, fresh perspectives, lessons in humility, and for making me feel 20 again. ❤️

Tagging my final project besties: Cyntia Jasmine, Johan Maurits S Sianipar, Arief Yunansyah, Mika Suryofakhri Rahwono, and Muhammad Yusuf 🥰

Don’t just follow job openings. Follow where the jobs are being created.

I was recently in transit in Manila on my way to another business trip and had my flight delayed because of the ASEAN Summit.

With leaders from Southeast Asia, Canada, Brazil, China and the US gathering in Manila, followed by the APEC Summit in Shenzhen, it’s quite an important week for Asia.

Sometimes, it’s difficult to separate what I do for a living from politics and economics. After all, where companies invest often determines where the jobs are.

One of the most debated topics in the Philippines right now is Pax Silica.

For those who haven’t been following it, it’s a US-led initiative to secure supply chains for semiconductors, AI technology and critical minerals.

The proposed industrial hub in New Clark City could attract US$40–70 billion in investments and create over 130,000 jobs 

And we’re not necessarily talking about opportunities exclusively for Filipinos.

A development of this scale could attract international executives, engineers, technical specialists and foreign companies, creating opportunities well beyond the semiconductor industry.

Having spent much of my professional life in China, I’ve seen how industrial investment can transform a country’s job market and attract talent from around the world.

When international companies explore Southeast Asia, Vietnam, Indonesia and Malaysia frequently come up. The Philippines deserves a closer look too, beyond outsourcing.

We already have an established semiconductor industry and a globally experienced workforce.

Of course, as a Filipino, I also have my reservations.

The Philippines has historically been more aligned with the US, while China remains a major economic partner despite ongoing maritime disputes.

Our geographical location makes us strategically important, but reducing dependence on China shouldn’t mean becoming overly dependent on the US.

The terms of investment, technology transfer and benefits to local industries and communities matter just as much as the number of jobs projected.

Why am I writing about this here?

I speak with professionals every day who are looking for their next opportunity, often in another country, yet spend very little time following what’s happening in those markets.

If you’re an engineer, a technology executive or a manufacturing professional looking to work in Asia, developments like Pax Silica are worth following.

The same applies to businesses exploring their next expansion market.

For a country that has spent decades sending talent overseas, it would be interesting to see the Philippines become a destination for international talent itself.

By the time hundreds of vacancies appear on job boards the investment decisions behind those jobs may have been made years earlier.

Your next career opportunity might already be taking shape somewhere in the world, long before it becomes a job opening.

Wed is here, and another #CeritaRecruiter from me
From Chemical Engineering to Recruitment. Who Would Have Thought? 

One question I often get when people learn about my educational background:
"Wait, you studied CHEMICAL ENGINEERING? How did you end up in recruitment?"
Well, life doesn't always go according to the degree we earned! 
Yes, I graduated in Chemical Engineering fromInstitut Teknologi Sepuluh Nopember (ITS), before pursuing my MBA in National Taiwan University of Science and Technology Taiwan.
And no, I didn't end up designing chemical plants or working in a laboratory.
Instead, I somehow ended up spending the past 14 years in recruitment!
But was my engineering education wasted?
ABSOLUTELY NOT.

In my early years atMonroe Consulting Group, I specialised in Industrial recruitment. Having a technical background certainly helped me understand the industries, the engineering terminology, and the technical requirements of the positions I was recruiting for.
But as my career progressed, from consultant to division leadership and eventually Managing Director, I realised something.
Your degree may determine where you start, but it doesn't have to determine where you end up
I've met so many incredible professionals who started in one discipline, moved into something completely different, and became exceptionally good at it.
What made the difference?
Their willingness to LEARN.
Satya Nadella, CEO of Microsoft, famously championed the shift from a "know-it-all" culture to a "learn-it-all" culture.
And I couldn't agree more.
We don't need to know everything when we begin.
We need curiosity, adaptability, humility, and the willingness to keep learning, even when we think we've already figured things out.
Because the moment we stop learning, we stop growing.
Which brings me to something very special.
I'm incredibly honoured to be featured in the November 2026 edition of Kampus Indonesia, highlighting the achievements and contributions of IKA ITS
Looking at the accomplished individuals featured alongside me, I feel both humbled and proud.

To my beloved alma mater, THANK YOU. 
For the education, the discipline, the problem-solving mindset, and the foundation that has stayed with me, even in a career far removed from Chemical Engineering.
I may not have become a chemical engineer by profession, but I will always be an engineer by education and by the way I approach challenges.
Proud to be an ITS alumna!
VIVAT ITS!! 
And to anyone considering a career outside their field of study:
Your degree is your foundation not your limitation

The most dangerous device in your office has been printing slides for five years
My feed this morning: "digital apocalypse", Apple, Microsoft, banks and airlines all down at once. 

Before forwarding, I checked.
What actually happened (as of 18 Nov) 
– 13 Nov: Microsoft 365 (Outlook, Teams) down in 70+ countries, into a second day. Microsoft: a technical issue, not cyber. 
– Within days: FAA, United Airlines, Marriott, Charles Schwab, even the NSA's classified internal network. 
– 17 Nov: App Store, iCloud, Apple Pay. Apple blames an internal update; its stores could not ring up sales. 
– US Secretary of State Rubio: "zero evidence" of a malign actor.

So no apocalypse. In a way it is worse: a week of self-inflicted failures showed how few points the world hangs on. A bad update did for free what an attacker would pay for.
Now the part nobody is posting about.

1) Everything above is IT: email, cloud, apps. Painful, but recoverable. OT is the systems that open valves, switch substations and run production lines. There a failure is not an error page. It is darkness, no water, a stopped plant.

2) The way in is rarely the front door. Back in 2019 Microsoft described a state-backed group entering corporate networks through an office printer, a VoIP phone and a video decoder. The printer that has faithfully printed your board decks for five years: default password, no update since installation, on the same flat network as everything else.

3) From the printer to SCADA is a question of segmentation. Dragos found poor IT/OT segmentation in 81% of its 2025 assessments; 73% of its incident cases involved stolen VPN or jump-host credentials. 3,300 industrial companies were hit by ransomware in 2025.

4) It has been done. December 2015, Ukraine: attackers took over SCADA at regional power distributors, and around 225,000 customers lost electricity.

In SEA the cybersecurity conversation still starts and ends with the IT department and a firewall budget. OT sits with engineers who have never met the CISO. Attackers do not respect that org chart.
This week the world went down by accident. 
The question for any CEO running a plant, a grid or a network: who in your company knows exactly what is connected to the production network? 
And when was the printer last updated?

Engineers, maintenance teams and buyers from these sites can reach BITEC without international travel. Visitors from Singapore, China, India, Malaysia and Indonesia, the main visitor markets at past editions, are a short flight away.

🔋 Batteries for short-term flexibility. Fast grid response and smooth management of daytime fluctuations, keeping mining and industrial operations stable and continuous.

The opportunity for Indonesia is clear: move from standard renewable installations to fully dispatchable power systems that run reliably, day and night.
